5116.t: Compound of φαλός (phalós, “white”) + ἄκρος (ákros, “topmost”). Akin to φάλαρος (phálaros).

5139.t: A medical expression. Formally it may be compared with ὑστέρα (hustéra, “uterus, womb”) and names of diseases like ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”) and ὕδερος (húderos, “dropsy”).

5135.t: The irregular form and suffix -ιδ- (-id-) lead Beekes to suggest a Mediterranean Pre-Greek origin, as he doesn't find a connection to Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to cry out”) (cognate with Middle High German glien (“to cry”), Old High German gellan (“to…

5113.t: Traditionally from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, plank”), with cognates such as Latin sufflāmen and Old High German balcho, but regular derivation of φάλαγγ- (phắlăng-) from this root is phonetically impossible, and the suffix is prototypical of…

5112.t: From Proto-Hellenic *térptis, from Proto-Indo-European *térptis (“fulfillment; satisfaction”); by surface analysis, τέρπω (térpō, “to satisfy”) + -σις (-sĭs).

5125.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰil- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *bʰil-o-s Ancient Greek φίλος (phĭ́los) Ancient Greek σοφός (sophós) Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος From φίλος (phĭ́los, “loving”) + σοφός (sophós, “wise”).

5134.t: From χαράσσω (kharássō, “to scratch, engrave”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, agent noun suffix). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀏𐀨𐀏𐀳𐀨 (ka-ra-ka-te-ra).

5131.t: Unclear etymology, but most likely derived from Proto-Hellenic *pʰármakon. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀔𐀒 (pa-ma-ko /⁠pʰármakon⁠/).

5117.t: From φαρμακεύω (pharmakeúō, “to use drugs”) + -ία (-ía), from φάρμακον (phármakon).

5114.t: From φιλέω (phĭléō, “to love; to kiss”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument noun suffix).

5163.t: From ἀθλέω (āthléō, “to contend”) + -τής (-tḗs, masculine agentive suffix).

5172.t: It matches Thracian Ἀλαζών (Alazṓn) exactly, perhaps an appellative, or it may be a cultural loanword from Akkadian 𒀀𒇻𒍣𒉡 aluzinnu, 'boastful, clownish fraud, most times pretending or claiming to possess medical skills or knowledge.' From Sumerian 𒀩𒍪…

5176.t: From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μέθυστος (méthŭstos, “drunken”), from μεθύω (methŭ́ō, “to be drunk on wine”), from μέθυ (méthŭ, “wine”). Compare to εὐμέθυστος (euméthŭstos, “easily made drunk”).

5156.t: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of ψάω (psā́ō, “to rub, wipe”), ψωμός (psōmós, “morsel, bit”), ψωλός (psōlós, “circumcised”), ψωρός (psōrós, “itchy; mangy”) and ψωχός (psōkhós, “sandy”).

5192.t: From ἀνδρεῖος (andreîos, “manly”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun–forming suffix). Compare ἠνορέη (ēnoréē).

5138.t: From χλεύη (khleúē, “jest, joke”) + -άζω (-ázō, suffix to form a verb).

5169.t: From ἄκρος (ắkros, “at the edge; extreme, outermost”) + πόλις (pólĭs, “city; the Athenian citadel”).

5185.t: From ἀνα- (“backwords”) + πούς (gentive: ποδός) (“foot”) + -ίζω (“suffix for verbs”).

5140.t: According to Beekes, of Pre-Greek origin.

5127.t: Unexplained. According to Beekes, the similarity of the suffix with κημός (kēmós, “muzzle”) is notable, while the relation with φιτρός (phitrós, “block of wood”) seems improbable.

5120.t: From φθείρω (phtheírō, “to spoil, ruin”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

5141.t: There is no exact outer-Greek correspondance to the verb, but the root *gʰrem- (“to resound, thunder, grumble, roar”) is Proto-Indo-European.

5187.t: From ἀνα- (ana-, intensifying affix) + σπάω (spáō, “to draw”)
